claims.text: Conventional pure Pt catalysts are highly active for hydrogen electrochemistry.
Conventional pure Pt catalysts suffer from high cost.
Conventional pure Pt catalysts have limited long-term durability under aggressive electrochemical cycling.
Co-alloying Pt with earth-abundant transition metals such as Ni, Co, and Fe can produce a Pt-based high-entropy-alloy catalyst.
Co-alloying Pt with Ni, Co, and Fe creates a compositionally complex surface with a tailored d-band center.
Incorporating secondary elements into Pt adjusts the hydrogen binding energy.
Incorporating secondary elements into Pt mitigates surface degradation.
Strategic non-noble-metal doping modifies the Pt-based catalyst's surface d-band center and hydrogen adsorption energy.
Modification of the d-band center and hydrogen adsorption energy promotes more favorable adsorption and desorption kinetics for hydrogen intermediates.
The proposed electronic-structure modification increases resistance to catalyst degradation during cyclic operation.
A Pt-based HEA containing non-noble-metal dopants is expected to exhibit lower HER and HOR overpotentials than pure Pt.
A Pt-based HEA containing non-noble-metal dopants is expected to exhibit higher HER and HOR exchange current densities than pure Pt.
A Pt-based HEA containing non-noble-metal dopants is expected to retain performance better than pure Pt during extended potential cycling.
The proposed activity and durability improvements are anticipated in both acidic and alkaline HER/HOR environments within the catalyst's stability limits.
The magnitude of enhancement may depend on composition, alloying strategy, and operating environment.
Pure Pt and Pt-Ni-Co-Fe nanoparticles will be compared under identical electrochemical and potential-cycling tests.
Failure of the Pt-based HEA to produce a statistically significant reduction in overpotential and improved performance retention relative to pure Pt will falsify the hypothesis.
